content.text:
I submitted **part-based** with confidence 0.88. I used 41 of the 60 budget.

**Design:** I trained the learner on two tasks, L1-S1-M1 and L4-S2-M4. The free `compare` and `describe` commands showed two things that made a clean test possible:
- L4 gives the opposite answer to L1.
- The motor rules M1 and M4 use completely different buttons.

So the task L4-S1-M1 is made only of rules the learner already knows, yet it gives the same response as neither trained task on any input. That is where the two hypotheses predict opposite results.

**Results** (9 noisy tests per task; lower means faster learning):

| Test task | New rules | Highest overlap with a trained task | Mean examples needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| L4-S1-M1 | 0 | 0% | 20 |
| L1-S1-M2 | 1 | 75% | 29 |
| L2-S3-M2 | 3 | 56% | 46 |
| L2-S3-M3 | 3 | 19% | 43 |

Before any training, L4-S1-M1 needed about 30 examples, from 3 tests.

**Why part-based:**
- The task with 0% overlap but all-familiar rules was learned fastest. A holistic learner should have found it the hardest.
- The two tasks with 3 new rules cost about the same, even though their overlap was very different (56% vs 19%). A holistic learner should have learned the 56% one clearly faster.
- Cost went up with the number of new rules (0 < 1 < 3), which is what the part-based hypothesis predicts.

I kept confidence below 0.9 because single tests swing a lot (1 to 37 on the same task) and the untrained baseline rests on only 3 tests. Still, the full ordering matched part-based and went against holistic in both places where they disagree.
